Q5750.L1t: Older adults are a growing share of the population, and health services increasingly use digital channels to share information.
Q5750.L2t: Surveys of internet use have long shown that adoption is lower in older age groups than in younger ones.
Q5750.L3t: Whether an information source can reach a group depends on how many of that group actually have access to it, and among people over 65 only a minority are connected.
Q5750.L4t: Careful thought is needed because most people over 65 do not have internet access, so internet-based sources would miss the majority of them.
Q5750.L2f: Surveys of internet use have long shown that adoption is highest in the oldest age groups and lowest among teenagers.
Q5750.L3f: The main concern is that the internet is designed, produced and marketed mainly with younger users in mind, so older people are not its intended audience.
Q5750.L4f: Careful thought is needed because the internet is aimed at younger people, so it is not designed for the over-65s.

Q8305.L1t: Courts in different countries handle foreign legal materials, such as laws and judgments, in different ways.
Q8305.L2t: Incorporation and transformation are doctrines that describe how international law, especially treaty obligations, becomes part of domestic law.
Q8305.L3t: Unlike customary rules, a foreign court's judgment has no force within another state's territory by itself, so its recognition and enforcement need an agreed legal basis between the states concerned, such as a treaty arrangement.
Q8305.L4t: No, recognition of foreign judgments is not governed by those doctrines but depends on appropriate bilateral or multilateral treaties being in place.
Q8305.L2f: The doctrines of incorporation and transformation were developed to explain how domestic statutes become binding on foreign states.
Q8305.L3f: Foreign judgments are treated as a source of international law that enters domestic law only once a legislature has passed an act that converts them into national law.
Q8305.L4f: Foreign judgments are enforced on the basis of the doctrine of transformation, so they take effect domestically only after being transformed by legislation.

Q5460.L1t: The hearsay rule generally bars out-of-court statements offered to prove the truth of what they assert, subject to a number of exceptions.
Q5460.L2t: Under the federal rules, an opposing party's own statement is not hearsay when offered against that party.
Q5460.L3t: A statement is attributable to an employer if it was made by an employee on a matter within the scope of that employment while the relationship existed, and here the painter spoke about the company's own co-workers' construction work during the job.
Q5460.L4t: The objection will fail because the painter's statement about his co-workers' work was made within the scope of his employment and so is attributable to the company.
Q5460.L2f: The rule on statements by a party's employee applies only to statements made under oath in a formal proceeding.
Q5460.L3f: A statement by an employee can be used against the employer only if the employee personally took part in the negligent act, and the painter did not take part in the wall work.
Q5460.L4f: The objection will be sustained because the painter was not a participant in the negligent act, so his statement cannot be admitted against the company.
